pharm: Provides essential water-soluble B vitamins that serve as coenzymes in energy metabolism, nucleic acid synthesis, and red-cell and nervous-system function.
quick: One B-complex tablet/capsule daily, or as directed; deficiency doses are vitamin-specific
Take with food to improve tolerance and absorption
B vitamins (including folate) are recommended in pregnancy at appropriate doses
Compatible; B vitamins are recommended during breastfeeding
Water-soluble; generally safe, though some are removed by dialysis and may need supplementation
No specific adjustment for usual supplemental doses
Alcohol use increases requirements (especially thiamine, B1) and the need for supplementation
Usually none for routine supplementation; specific levels (e.g., B12, folate) when treating deficiency
summary: Vitamin B refers to the B-complex group of water-soluble vitamins - thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6), biotin (B7), folate (B9), and cobalamin (B12) - which act as essential coenzymes in metabolism, DNA synthesis, and red-cell and nerve function. B-complex supplements are used to prevent or treat deficiency states (e.g., poor diet, alcoholism, malabsorption, pregnancy) and as general nutritional support. Excess water-soluble B vitamins are largely excreted in urine, so toxicity is uncommon, though chronic high-dose pyridoxine (B6) can cause sensory neuropathy and high-dose niacin can cause flushing and hepatotoxicity.
indications: Prevention and treatment of vitamin B-complex deficiency (inadequate diet, alcoholism, malabsorption, increased demand)
Nutritional supplementation in pregnancy, lactation, and recovery/convalescence
Adjunctive support for conditions associated with B-vitamin deficiency (e.g., peripheral neuropathy, certain anemias)

dosage.d: One B-complex tablet/capsule once daily providing around the recommended daily allowances
dosage.n: Product strengths vary; follow the specific label

dosage.d: Mild: 25-100 mg/day orally; severe/Wernicke: high-dose parenteral thiamine per protocol
dosage.n: Give thiamine before glucose in suspected deficiency

dosage.d: Deficiency 10-50 mg/day; specific indications higher under supervision
dosage.n: Avoid chronic high doses (>100-200 mg/day) - neuropathy risk

dosage.d: B12 deficiency: 1000 mcg IM per schedule or high-dose oral; folate 1-5 mg/day
dosage.n: Confirm B12 status before folate-only therapy to avoid masking B12 deficiency

admin: Take with food and water to improve tolerance
Riboflavin (B2) commonly causes a harmless bright-yellow discoloration of the urine
For deficiency treatment, use the specific vitamin and dose appropriate to the deficiency
In suspected thiamine deficiency, administer thiamine before or with glucose loads
moa: The B vitamins act as essential cofactors/coenzymes: thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate) in carbohydrate metabolism; riboflavin and niacin in oxidation-reduction (FAD/FMN, NAD/NADP); pantothenic acid in coenzyme A; pyridoxine in amino-acid and neurotransmitter metabolism; biotin in carboxylation reactions; folate and cobalamin in one-carbon transfer, DNA synthesis, and erythropoiesis. Together they support energy production, nucleic-acid synthesis, and normal hematologic and neurologic function.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to a specific B vitamin or formulation component (e.g., cobalt for cyanocobalamin)
relative: Untreated B12 deficiency when giving folate alone (may mask/worsen neurologic damage)
Pre-existing peripheral neuropathy (caution with high-dose B6)
monitor: For deficiency therapy: relevant vitamin levels and hematologic response
Liver function and flushing with high-dose niacin

preg: B vitamins, including folate, are recommended during pregnancy at appropriate doses; folic acid supplementation reduces the risk of neural tube defects. Routine supplemental amounts are considered safe; avoid megadoses of individual B vitamins unless prescribed.
lact: B vitamins are compatible with breastfeeding and are recommended to maintain adequate maternal and infant nutrition; routine supplemental doses are safe.
renal: Water-soluble B vitamins are generally safe in renal impairment; some (e.g., folate, B6, B12) are removed during dialysis, so supplementation may be needed in dialysis patients.
hepatic: Usual supplemental doses require no adjustment; high-dose niacin (B3) can be hepatotoxic and should be used cautiously in liver disease.

major: High-dose niacin with statins (increased risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis - clinical significance debated)
moderate: Pyridoxine (B6) reduces levodopa effect (when given without a decarboxylase inhibitor)
Folate may lower phenytoin levels and reduce seizure control
Certain antibiotics/antiepileptics and metformin/PPIs can lower B-vitamin (B12, folate) levels, increasing need
minor: Riboflavin causes harmless yellow urine that can confuse some urine color-based observations
interactions.food: Take with food for tolerance; a balanced diet supplies most B vitamins.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use impairs absorption/utilization and increases requirements, especially thiamine.
interactions.diagnostics: High-dose biotin (B7) can cause clinically significant interference with many immunoassays (e.g., thyroid, troponin, hormone tests).

serious: Chronic high-dose pyridoxine (B6): sensory peripheral neuropathy
Severe hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (rare, mainly with parenteral B vitamins)
rare: Anaphylactoid reaction to parenteral thiamine or cyanocobalamin
Acne or rosacea-like eruption with very high B12 doses

monitoring: Routine supplementation usually needs no monitoring
When treating deficiency: relevant vitamin levels and hematologic response (CBC, reticulocytes)
Neurologic exam with prolonged high-dose pyridoxine
Liver enzymes, glucose, and uric acid with high-dose niacin
counsel: Take with food; a harmless bright-yellow urine from riboflavin is expected
Do not take very high doses of individual B vitamins long-term without advice (B6 can cause nerve problems; high-dose niacin can flush and affect the liver)
Tell your doctor you take biotin before blood tests, as it can interfere with results
A balanced diet usually provides enough B vitamins; supplements help if your diet is poor, you drink alcohol heavily, are pregnant, or have absorption problems
If you have anemia or nerve symptoms, see a clinician so the right vitamin and dose are used
pk: Absorbed from the upper GI tract over hours; clinical benefit in deficiency over days to weeks
Blood levels typically peak within 1-2 hours of an oral dose
Varies by vitamin (hours for most water-soluble B vitamins; B12 is stored in the liver for years)
Water-soluble - excess is excreted in urine; daily intake maintains levels
Store in a cool, dry place protected from light and moisture; keep tightly closed
pearls: NOTE: 'Vitamin B' is treated here as a B-complex dietary supplement; content is reference-sourced (dietary-reference and pharmacology references) rather than from a single FDA drug label
Water-soluble, so excess is largely excreted - acute toxicity is uncommon
High-dose pyridoxine (B6) can cause a dose-dependent sensory neuropathy - avoid chronic megadoses
Give thiamine (B1) before glucose in suspected deficiency to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Do not treat suspected B12 deficiency with folate alone - it can mask anemia while neurologic damage progresses; high-dose biotin interferes with many lab immunoassays
missed: For routine daily supplementation, take the missed dose when remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Acute overdose of most water-soluble B vitamins is usually mild because the excess is excreted in urine. However, chronic excess of specific vitamins can be harmful: high-dose pyridoxine (B6) causes sensory neuropathy, high-dose niacin (B3) causes flushing, hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia, and high-dose biotin interferes with laboratory tests. Management is to stop the supplement and provide supportive care; symptoms of B6 neuropathy may improve slowly after discontinuation.
